Serving two terms as Congress President in the 1920s, this Indian independence-era lawyer and activist was the patriarch of a famous political dynasty and father to India's first prime minister — who was he?
Motilal Nehru: Indian lawyer and politician (1861–1931)

Famous for aggressive cavalry tactics and a rapid rise from private to general, this Confederate officer — a pre-war slave trader — became the first Grand Wizard of the Reconstruction-era Ku Klux Klan. Who was he?
Nathan Bedford Forrest: Confederate States Army general, farmer and Ku Klux Klan leader (1821–1877)

Once jailed as a suspected war criminal after WWII, this man returned to power as Japan's prime minister and forced through a revised U.S. security treaty before the Anpo protests drove him out — who was he?
Nobusuke Kishi: Prime Minister of Japan from 1957 to 1960.
This legendary Thracian musician could charm even stones with his lyre, sailed with Jason in search of the Golden Fleece, and journeyed into the underworld to reclaim his dead wife — who is he?
Orpheus: Legendary musician, poet, and prophet in Greek mythology.
This Finnish Green League politician served as Foreign Minister from 2019 to 2023 and became the first openly gay candidate to run for his country's presidency — who is he?
Once married to a future Roman emperor, this woman went on to become Nero's second wife, and a lavish excavated villa near Pompeii bears her name — who is she?
Poppaea Sabina: Roman empress from 62 to 65 AD.

Founded in 1891 by Leandro N. Alem, this Argentine political party is the country's second-oldest active party and a longtime human-rights advocate that has been banned under military rule — which party?
Radical Civic Union: Political party in Argentina. The Radical Civic Union (Spanish: Unión Cívica Radical, UCR) is a major political party in Argentina.
Sparked by an 1835 revolt against a Mexican president's new centralizing constitution, this sovereign nation lasted barely a decade before joining a much larger union — what was it?
Republic of Texas: Country in North America (1836–1846)
This U.S. Army officer led E Company's assault on the Belgian town of Foy after the siege of Bastogne was broken, and later served as the American governor of a Berlin prison — who is he?
A native of Zanzibar, she became Tanzania's first woman president in 2021 after ascending from the vice-presidency on her predecessor's death. Who is she?
Samia Suluhu Hassan: President of Tanzania since 2021. A native of Zanzibar, Suluhu served as a minister in the semi-autonomous region from 2000 to 2010.
Nicknamed "the Grim," this Ottoman sultan grew his empire by seventy percent in just eight years, conquering the entire Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt between 1516 and 1517 — who was he?
Selim I: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1512 to 1520.
After a 1969 coup, this army commander became Somalia's third president and reconstituted the country as a one-party Marxist-Leninist state — who is he?
Siad Barre: President of Somalia from 1969 to 1991.
Based on the island of Sumatra, this maritime empire became a key center for spreading Buddhism across Southeast Asia between the 7th and 11th centuries — which empire?
Srivijaya: Empire based on Sumatra (c. 671–1025 AD)
Representing the Goshamahal constituency in Hyderabad, this Indian politician served as a state assembly whip for the BJP in Telangana until 2025 — who is he?
T. Raja Singh: Indian politician. Thakur Raja Singh (born 15 April 1977) is an Indian politician from the state of Telangana.

Fought entirely on Carthaginian soil after King Masinissa's repeated raids provoked a doomed counterattack under Hasdrubal, which 149-146 BC conflict was the last and final clash between Rome and Carthage?
Third Punic War: War between Rome and Carthage (149–146 BC). The war was fought entirely within Carthaginian territory, in what is now northern Tunisia.
This branch of Marxism-Leninism is named for the Russian revolutionary who developed it alongside the Left Opposition and the Fourth International — what's it called?
Trotskyism: Variety of Marxism developed by Leon Trotsky.
The last man standing in the Year of the Four Emperors, this Roman founded the Flavian dynasty and was the first emperor to rise from an equestrian family. Who was he?
Vespasian: Roman emperor from AD 69 to 79.
Sometimes anachronistically called Elizabeth, this woman was empress consort to China's last emperor before later becoming empress consort of the Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo — who was she?
Wanrong: Empress of Manchukuo from 1934 to 1945 (1906–1946)
Alongside Andrew Moray, this Scottish knight won the Battle of Stirling Bridge in 1297 before being captured and executed for treason in 1305 — who is he?
William Wallace: Scottish knight (1270–1305). Along with Andrew Moray, Wallace defeated an English army at the Battle of Stirling Bridge in September 1297.
October 1973: the holiest day of the Jewish calendar collided with the 10th day of Ramadan when Arab forces launched a surprise attack on Israel. What war broke out?
Yom Kippur War: 1973 war between Israel and Arab states.
Who among these was born first?
Benjamin Banneker (born 1731) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the eldest?

Sergei Krikalev (born 1958) is the earliest of the four. Sergei Konstantinovich Krikalev (Russian: Сергей Константинович Крикалёв; born 27 August 1958) is a Russian mechanical engineer and former cosmonaut.
Which of these was founded earliest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four. COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language;) is a compiled English-like computer programming language designed for business use.
Which of these was founded earliest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the physicist from these four.
Norman Ramsey Jr. is a physicist.
Who among these is a chemist?
Ivan Pavlov is a chemist. Pavlov also conducted significant research on the physiology of digestion, for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1904.
What is the atomic number of Oganesson?
Oganesson is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Og and atomic number 118.
In what year was Michael Rockefeller born?
Michael Rockefeller: Michael Clark Rockefeller (May 18, 1938; disappeared November 19, 1961) was an American anthropologist and art collector and member of the Rockefeller family.
In what year was William James Sidis born?
William James Sidis: Born to Boris Sidis, a prominent psychiatrist, and Sarah Mandelbaum Sidis, a physician, Sidis demonstrated extraordinary intellectual capabilities from infancy.
In what year was Wernher von Braun born?
Wernher von Braun: As a young man, von Braun worked in Nazi Germany's rocket development program.
In what year did Carl Linnaeus die?
Carl Linnaeus: Linnaeus was the son of a curate and was born in Råshult, in the countryside of Småland, southern Sweden.
In what year did Antoine Lavoisier die?
Antoine Lavoisier: It is generally accepted that Lavoisier's great accomplishments in chemistry stem largely from his changing the science from a qualitative to a quantitative one.
In what year was Palladium discovered?
Palladium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Pd and atomic number 46.
In what year was Chromium discovered?
Chromium is a chemical element; it has symbol Cr and atomic number 24.
Mil Mi-28: Mil Moscow Helicopter Plant. The Mil Mi-28 (NATO reporting name "Havoc") is a Soviet heavy-weight, all-weather, day-night, tandem-seat anti-armour military attack helicopter.
In which country did the Hawker Hurricane take place?
Hawker Hurricane: United Kingdom. The Air Ministry ordered Hawker's Interceptor Monoplane in late 1934, and the prototype Hurricane K5083 performed its maiden flight on 6 November 1935.
Who is credited with discovering Telescopium?
Telescopium: Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. Its name is a Latinized form of the Greek word for telescope.
Who is credited with discovering Spontaneous generation?
Spontaneous generation: Anaximander. It was hypothesized that certain forms, such as fleas, could arise from inanimate matter such as dust, or that maggots could arise from dead flesh.
Who is credited with discovering SN 1987A?
SN 1987A: Ian Shelton. SN 1987A was a Type II supernova in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.
This Onmyōdō master advised Heian emperors on astrology and spiritual matters; a Kyoto shrine and an Osaka train station now honor him — who is he?
Abe no Seimei (February 21, 921 AD - October 31, 1005) was a Japanese onmyji, a court official and specialist of Onmyd, during the middle of the Heian period.
Which diverse group of aquatic photosynthetic organisms excludes land plants but includes seaweeds that can grow up to 50 metres long?
Algae (UK also; sing.: alga) are any of a large and diverse group of photosynthetic organisms.
This type of long-term arthritis causes inflammation where the spine meets the pelvis, with lower back pain as its hallmark symptom. What condition is it?
Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a type of arthritis from the disease spectrum of axial spondyloarthritis.

This German philosopher's 1818 masterwork describes the visible world as the manifestation of a blind, irrational underlying will, building on Kantian idealism while rejecting German idealism's optimism — who is he?
Arthur Schopenhauer (22 February 1788 - 21 September 1860) was a German philosopher and writer.
The first production aircraft of its type, this American military transport combines vertical takeoff and landing with long-range cruise performance—what is it?
Bell Boeing V-22 Osprey is an American multi-use, tiltrotor military transport and cargo aircraft with both vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) and short takeoff and landing (STOL) capabilities.
In service with the U.S. Air Force since 1955 — and flown by NASA until 2007 — this subsonic strategic bomber can haul 70,000 pounds of weapons nearly 8,800 miles without refueling. Which aircraft?
Boeing B-52 Stratofortress is an American nuclear-capable subsonic jet-powered strategic bomber.
This Indian physicist discovered, with his student, that light changes wavelength when passing through a transparent material — a phenomenon now named for him — earning a 1930 Nobel Prize. Who is he?
C. V. Raman (7 November 1888 - 21 November 1970) was an Indian physicist known for his work in the field of light scattering.
A flightless ratite native to the tropical forests of New Guinea and northeastern Australia, this large bird has three living species and lacks a keel on its breastbone — name the bird?
Cassowary (Tok) are flightless birds of the genus Casuarius, in the order Casuariiformes.
Made of DNA wound around histone proteins, this substance shapes chromosomes into their distinctive forms during cell division and gatekeeps access to genes for transcription and repair — what is it?
Chromatin is a complex of DNA and protein responsible for condensing and packaging chromosomal DNA.
With algorithms and data structures at its core and the theory of computation among its branches, which field studies computation, information, and automation?

Computer science is the study of computation, information, and automation. The theory of computation concerns abstract models of computation and general classes of problems that can be solved using them.
Named after the bladder it was first found in, which amino acid carries a thiol side chain that forms the disulfide bonds holding many proteins together?
Cysteine (symbol Cys or C) is a semiessential proteinogenic amino acid with the formula HSCH2CH(NH2)COOH.
Domesticated over 14,000 years ago — before farming even began — this descendant of wolves shares a common ancestor with the modern gray wolf. What animal is it?
Dog (Canis familiaris or Canis lupus familiaris) is a domesticated descendant of wolves.
Which American toy magnate teamed up with his wife Ruth to co-found Mattel and dream up Hot Wheels and Barbie?
Elliot Handler (April 9, 1916 - July 21, 2011) was an American inventor, business magnate, and the co-founder of Mattel.
Genus Vespa's largest eusocial wasp, this insect was introduced to North America as early as 1840 and remains the only true member of its genus found there — what is it?
European hornet (Vespa crabro) is the largest eusocial wasp native to Europe.
This genus in the rose family includes more than 20 species prized for their sweet-to-tart edible fruits, with domestic hybrids grown worldwide — what is its scientific name?
Fragaria is a genus of flowering plants in the rose family, Rosaceae, commonly known as strawberries for their edible fruits.

Sometimes called the 'lesser apes' to distinguish them from chimpanzees, gorillas, and orangutans, these smaller, tailless primates live in forests from eastern Bangladesh through Southeast Asia and don't build nests — what are they?
Gibbon are apes in the family Hylobatidae (hylobatids).
Named from Ancient Greek words for 'blood' and 'to make,' this biological process produces up to a hundred billion new blood cells per day in a healthy adult — what is it?
Haematopoiesis (from Ancient Greek (hama) 'blood' and (poien) 'to make'; also hematopoiesis in US English, sometimes h(a)emopoiesis) is the formation of blood cellular components.

Discovered in 2013 deep in South Africa's Rising Star Cave system, this archaic human left behind over 1,500 bones from at least 15 individuals, yet a tiny brain keeps its place in our family tree a puzzle — what species is it?

Homo naledi is an extinct species of archaic human discovered in 2013 in the Rising Star Cave system, Gauteng province, South Africa, part of the Cradle of Humankind, dating back to the Middle Pleistocene 335,000-236,000 years ago.
Aided by Soviet intelligence gathered on the American Manhattan Project, this physicist oversaw the first Soviet nuclear weapon test at Semipalatinsk in 1949 — who is he?
Igor Kurchatov was Soviet nuclear physicist (1903–1960).
The first woman ever to chair the Federal Reserve, she later became the first woman to serve as U.S. Treasury secretary — a Brooklyn-born, Yale-trained economist. Who is she?
Janet Yellen (born August 13, 1946) is an American economist who served as the 78th United States secretary of the treasury from 2021 to 2025 and as chair of the Federal Reserve from 2014 to 2018.

Sharing the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, this ethologist was among the first to decode the honey bee's waggle dance — a theory greeted with such skepticism that it took decades to be vindicated. Who was he?
Karl von Frisch (20 November 1886 - 12 June 1982) was a German-Austrian ethologist who received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973, along with Nikolaas Tinbergen and Konrad Lorenz.

A hybrid of the citron and the bitter orange believed to have originated in northeastern India around the 1st millennium BC, this small evergreen citrus tree bears a tart yellow fruit used worldwide — name the fruit?
Lemon (Citrus limon) is a species of small evergreen tree in the Citrus genus of the flowering plant family Rutaceae.
Named for a Dutch physicist, this six-parameter family of linear equations converts spacetime coordinates between reference frames moving at constant relative velocity — what is it?
Lorentz transformation are a six-parameter family of linear transformations from a coordinate frame in spacetime to another frame that moves at a constant velocity relative to the former.
Following fieldwork with the Omaha people and in Papua New Guinea and Bali, this anthropologist explored gender roles in her 1935 book Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies — who is she?
Margaret Mead (December 16, 1901 - November 15, 1978) was an American cultural anthropologist, author and speaker, who appeared frequently in the mass media during the mid-twentieth century.
This field's founding body, the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures, grew out of an 1875 convention and eventually gave the world the International System of Units — what is this study called?
Metrology is the scientific study of measurement.
A demyelinating disease whose relapsing-remitting form shows up in about 85% of patients, it can cause double vision, muscle weakness, and loss of coordination — what is it?
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks myelin, the insulating cover of nerve cells in the human body, causing damage to one's own central nervous system.
Element 113, a synthetic and ferociously radioactive member of the periodic table, was confirmed by a team at Riken in Japan — what's its name?
Nihonium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Nh and atomic number 113.

Sitting in life's hierarchy between tissue and a full body system, this term describes a group of different tissues — like the epithelial and muscle layers of the gut wall — joined to serve one shared function. What is it?
Organ (biology) is a collection of tissues joined in a structural unit to serve a common function.
Which American biologist became famous for the controversial 1968 book 'The Population Bomb' and its dire warnings about population growth, famine, and resource depletion?

Paul R. Ehrlich (May 29, 1932 - March 13, 2026) was an American biologist, author, and environmentalist known for his predictions and warnings about the consequences of population growth, including famine and resource depletion.
With a musty odor like freshly cut hay, this toxic colorless gas is the double acyl-chloride cousin of carbonic acid, and it saw grim use as a chemical weapon in World War I. Name the compound?
Phosgene is an organic chemical compound with the formula COCl2.
Native to cool temperate regions of the Old World, which poplar species is commonly known as European or quaking aspen?
Populus tremula (commonly called aspen, common aspen, Eurasian aspen, European aspen, or quaking aspen) is a species of poplar native to cool temperate regions of the Old World.
Like a cosmic lighthouse, this highly magnetized, rapidly rotating neutron star is only visible from Earth when its beam of radiation sweeps directly toward us — what's the object?
Pulsar (pulsating star, on the model of quasar) is a highly magnetized rotating neutron star that emits beams of electromagnetic radiation out of its magnetic poles.
Which large Southern African dog breed, whose standard was drafted in 1922 in what's now Zimbabwe, descends from ridged hunting dogs of the Khoikhoi crossed with European breeds used to bay lions?
Rhodesian Ridgeback is a large dog breed originally bred in Southern Africa.
This Harvard political scientist argued in a 1993 theory that future conflict would erupt not between countries but between cultures — a 'clash of civilizations.' Who was he?
Samuel P. Huntington (April 18, 1927 - December 24, 2008) was an American political scientist, adviser, and academic.
The smallest of Japan's six native dog breeds, this small, alert hunting dog's name literally translates to 'brushwood dog,' reflecting its original job of flushing game — which breed?
Shiba Inu (Japanese) is a breed of hunting dog from Japan.

Extending from the base of the brainstem down to the lower back, this tubular bundle of nervous tissue is covered by the meninges and, together with the brain, makes up the central nervous system — name this structure?

Spinal cord is a long, thin, tubular structure made up of nervous tissue that extends from the medulla oblongata in the lower brainstem to the lumbar region of the vertebral column (backbone) of vertebrate animals.
A starchy tuber from the morning-glory family, often confused with yams in North America despite being only distantly related to them — what root vegetable is it?
Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) is a dicotyledonous plant in the morning glory family, Convolvulaceae.
This part of the lower limb sits between the hip and the knee, containing a single thick bone — the femur — that forms a ball-and-socket joint above and a hinge joint below — name the body part?
Thigh is the area between the hip (pelvis) and the knee.

Native only to New Zealand and resembling a lizard, this reptile is the sole surviving member of an order that was hugely diverse in the Mesozoic era, with fossils dating to the Middle Triassic — what's the animal?
Tuatara (Mori:; Sphenodon punctatus) is a species of reptile endemic to New Zealand.

First described by John Edward Gray in 1821, this family of small feliform mammals spans Africa, southern Europe, and Asia on both sides of the Wallace Line, and includes the genets — name the family?
Viverridae is a family of small to medium-sized feliform mammals, comprising 14 genera with 33 species.
Native from Panama to southern Canada, this plant genus of 50 species belongs to the asparagus family alongside the agaves — name the genus?
Yucca (YUK-) is both the scientific name and common name for a genus native to North America from Panama to southern Canada.
This protrusion in the neck, formed by the angle of the thyroid cartilage around the larynx, becomes more prominent in most men during puberty — what is it?
Adam's apple: Feature of the neck. The Adam's apple is the protrusion in the neck formed by the angle of the thyroid cartilage surrounding the larynx, typically visible in men and less so in women.

This organic functional group, structured R−CH=O and alternatively called a formyl group when isolated from its side chain, appears throughout biologically and technologically important chemicals — what is it?
Aldehyde: Organic compound containing the functional group R–CH=O.

Once sold as Elavil, this tricyclic antidepressant is now often a second-line choice — used as much for neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, and migraines as for depression, thanks to its many side effects. Which drug?
Amitriptyline: Tricyclic antidepressant. Due to the frequency and prominence of side effects, amitriptyline is generally considered a second-line therapy for these indications.
Awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2008 for his AIDS-relief work on PEPFAR, this immunologist directed the U.S. allergy and infectious-disease institute from 1984 to 2022. Who is he?
A notoriously toxic metalloid and pnictogen with atomic number 33, it's used in lead alloys for car batteries and ammunition and as a semiconductor dopant — which element is it?
Arsenic: Chemical element with atomic number 33 (As). It is a metalloid and one of the pnictogens, and therefore shares many properties with its group 15 neighbors phosphorus and antimony.
This slender projection of a nerve cell typically carries electrical impulses away from the cell body toward other neurons, muscles, or glands — what is it called?
Axon: Long projection on a neuron that conducts signals to other neurons.
A colorless, sweet-smelling liquid hiding in petroleum, this ring-shaped hydrocarbon helps give gasoline its distinctive aroma — what is it?
Composed of plasma plus red cells, white cells, and platelets, this circulatory fluid delivers oxygen and nutrients to the body while carrying away waste — what is it?
Blood: Body fluid in the circulatory system. Plasma, which constitutes 55% of blood fluid, is mostly water (92% by volume), and contains proteins, glucose, mineral ions, and hormones.
This plant family — nicknamed the mustards or crucifers, and including cabbage — hosts the caterpillars of a notorious garden-pest butterfly as one of its worst enemies — name the family?

Ranging from the hefty black species of the Amazon basin to the diminutive dwarf species just over a metre long, these Central and South American relatives of alligators make up their own reptile subfamily — what are they called?
Caiman: Subfamily of reptiles. The black caiman is the largest caiman species in the world and is found in the slow-moving rivers and lakes that surround the Amazon basin.

Born in London, raised in Milan, and self-taught in web design, this Catholic teenager built a website cataloguing Eucharistic miracles before dying of leukemia at fifteen — he was beatified in 2020. Who was he?
Which second-generation antihistamine for hay fever kicks in within half an hour but is more likely than fexofenadine or loratadine to cause drowsiness?

Cetirizine: Antihistamine medication. Cetirizine is a second-generation peripherally selective antihistamine used to treat allergic rhinitis (hay fever), dermatitis, urticaria (hives), and runny nose.
This plant genus includes both chicory, whose roasted roots make a coffee substitute, and true endive, the base for salad greens like escarole — which genus?
Cichorium: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae.

Believed to be the first coffee species ever cultivated, this plant, native to the forests of Ethiopia, South Sudan, and Yemen, still accounts for roughly 60% of global coffee production — what's its scientific name?
Coffea arabica: Species of coffee plant. Coffea arabica, also known as the Arabica coffee, is a species of flowering plant in the coffee and madder family Rubiaceae.
Found only in placental mammals, this roughly four-inch bundle of 200 to 300 million nerve fibers is the brain's largest white-matter structure, linking its left and right hemispheres — what is it?
Corpus callosum: White matter tract connecting the two cerebral hemispheres.
Inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, this disorder coats the lungs and other organs in thick mucus, inviting repeated bacterial infections — what genetic condition is it?
Cystic fibrosis: Genetic disorder affecting mostly the lungs.

Doctors once spotted this endocrine condition by its three Ps — polydipsia, polyuria, and polyphagia, or excessive thirst, urination, and hunger — all tracing back to trouble with insulin. Which disease is it?
Diabetes: Group of endocrine diseases characterized by high blood sugar levels.

Aristotle's Poetics contrasted this performance-based mode with the epic and the lyrical, and its name comes from a Greek word meaning "deed" or "act" — the two-masks symbol marks its split into comedy and tragedy. What is it?
Drama: Artwork intended for performance; formal type of literature.
The largest living land animal comes in three recognized species and counts mammoths and mastodons among its extinct cousins — what is it?
Elephant: Largest living land animal. The trunk is prehensile, bringing food and water to the mouth and grasping objects.
Marketed as Lexapro, this SSRI treats depression and anxiety but is exclusively sold commercially as an oxalate salt — what is it?

Escitalopram: SSRI antidepressant. It is mainly used to treat major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD), and social anxiety disorder.
With a black-tipped bushy tail and brownish-grey striped fur, this small wild feline lives in Scotland, Turkey, the Caucasus, and mainland forests, hunting rodents and ground birds — which species?
European wildcat: Small wild cat. The European wildcat (Felis silvestris) is a small wildcat species that was described in the late 18th century.
This genus of over 200 stinging insect species, Solenopsis, includes 'ginger' and 'tropical' varieties named for their painful bite and reddish coloring — what are they commonly called?
Fire ant: Genus of red ants.
This cold-weather injury turns skin white or waxy-blue after tissue actually freezes, often preceded by a tingling, numb warning stage called frostnip — what is it?
Frostbite: Effect of low temperature on skin and other tissues.
Named from Greek words for 'old man' and 'healer,' this medical specialty focuses on preventing and treating disease in older adults with no fixed age cutoff — what is it called?
Geriatrics: Medical specialty that focuses on health care of elderly people.
This cluster of immune cells forms around bacteria, fungi, or foreign material the body can't otherwise clear away — what is it called?
Granuloma: Inflammatory aggregation of immune cells.

This British aviation entrepreneur held three Guinness World Records after visiting the South Pole, the Challenger Deep, and space, then died in 2023 aboard the submersible that imploded near the Titanic wreck — who was he?
Using only a triangle's three side lengths and their semiperimeter, this ancient geometric method computes the triangle's area — what is it known as?
Heron's formula: Triangle area in terms of side lengths.
Generally colourless, hydrophobic, and faintly gasoline-scented, which organic compound is made entirely of hydrogen and carbon and includes everything from methane to paraffin wax?

Hydrocarbon: Organic compound consisting entirely of hydrogen and carbon. In the fossil fuel industries, hydrocarbon refers to naturally occurring petroleum, natural gas and coal, or their hydrocarbon derivatives and purified forms.
Designed in 1967 to replace the An-12 and haul heavy machinery into remote, poorly served regions, this four-engine Soviet airlifter earned the NATO name 'Candid' — what is it?
Ilyushin Il-76: Russian heavy four-engined military transport jet aircraft.
The biggest cat in the Americas, it has a bite so powerful it can crack a turtle's shell or punch straight through a skull between the ears — which animal?
Jaguar: Large cat native to the Americas.
Trained originally in mathematics at Cambridge, this English economist's Depression-era writings became the foundation for a whole school of macroeconomic thought bearing his name — who is he?
This classical physics model imagines matter as countless invisible particles in constant, random collisions, explaining pressure, temperature and viscosity alike — what is it?
Kinetic theory of gases: Understanding of gas properties in terms of molecular motion.

The smallest member of the genus Mustela, this slender carnivore has been introduced to New Zealand, Malta, Crete, the Azores, and São Tomé despite being native across Eurasia and North Africa — what is it?
Element number 3, this soft silvery-white alkali metal is the least dense metal of all and so reactive it must be stored under oil or in an inert atmosphere — what is it?
Lithium: Chemical element with atomic number 3 (Li)
Found in the hundreds inside most animal cells but almost never in plant cells, this acidic, enzyme-packed organelle serves as the cell's degradation center — which organelle?
Lysosome: Cell membrane organelle. A lysosome (/ˈlaɪsəˌsoʊm/) is a membrane-bound organelle that is found in all animal cells (except red blood cells), and rarely in plant cells.
The first Mexican-born scientist to win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, this physical chemist shared the 1995 award for revealing how CFC gases threaten the ozone layer — who?
Nicknamed 'meow meow' and chemically related to compounds in the khat plant, this synthetic stimulant produces effects similar to MDMA and was first synthesized in 1929 — which drug?
Mephedrone: Recreational drug. Mephedrone, also known as 4-methylmethcathinone, 4-MMC, or 4-methylephedrone, is a synthetic stimulant drug belonging to the amphetamine and cathinone classes.

Given the NATO reporting name 'Hip,' this Soviet-designed helicopter family has been in continuous production since 1975 as a medium twin-turbine transport, with an armed gunship variant — which aircraft?
Mil Mi-17: Family of Russian military transport helicopters.
Built with a slender segmented body and a long piercing-and-sucking proboscis, this family of 3,600 fly species diversified back in the Cretaceous — what are they?
Mosquito: Family of flies. The word mosquito (formed by mosca and diminutive -ito) is Spanish and Portuguese for little fly.

This branch of alternative medicine rests on vitalism and folk healing rather than evidence, and its grab-bag of 'natural' methods runs from the thoroughly discredited to certain accepted psychotherapies. What is it?
Naturopathy: Form of alternative medicine. The ethics of naturopathy have been called into question by medical professionals and its practice has been characterized as quackery.
Born in New York to Holocaust-survivor parents, this political scientist made the politics of the Holocaust and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict his life's work. Who is he?
This medical specialty trains physicians for four years after medical school to diagnose, medically treat, and surgically correct eye disease — what is it?
Ophthalmology: Field of medicine treating eye disorders.
Credited as the 'father of toxicology,' this Swiss Renaissance physician and alchemist also wrote prophetic 'Prognostications' later studied by Rosicrucians — who is he?
Paracelsus: Swiss physician, philosopher, theologian, and alchemist (c. 1493 – 1541)
Derived from the Latin for 'by a hundred,' this dimensionless number expresses a ratio as a fraction of 100 and is usually written with a % sign — what is it called?

Percentage: Number or ratio expressed as a fraction of 100. In mathematics, a percentage, percent, or per cent (from Latin per centum 'by a hundred') is a number or ratio expressed as a fraction of 100.
This healthcare profession uses patient education and hands-on interventions to prevent, treat, and restore mobility, with specialties from sports medicine to pediatrics — which field?
Physical therapy: Profession that helps a disabled person function in everyday life.
This large, structurally diverse family of plant compounds includes flavonoids and tannic acid, some of which were historically used as dyes and for tanning garments — what are they called?
Also called cherry laurel, this evergreen shrub native to the Black Sea region was once woven into wreaths for its resemblance to true bay laurel, though the two aren't closely related — which plant?
Prunus laurocerasus: Species of plant. It is not to be confused with its American relative Prunus caroliniana, which is also called cherry laurel.
The largest of the procyonid family, this North American mammal is famous for its facial mask, ringed tail, and remarkably dexterous front paws — which animal is it?
